# fyaml - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fyaml/0.5.2/fyaml/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#fyaml)fyaml

A safe Rust wrapper around the `libfyaml` C library for parsing and
manipulating YAML documents.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

`fyaml` provides an idiomatic Rust interface to the high-performance
`libfyaml` YAML parsing library. It supports DOM-style navigation,
zero-copy scalar access, node type introspection, multi-document
parsing, document mutation, and a serde-compatible `Value` type.

[§](https://docs.rs#status)Status

**Early development** - This library is functional but has not yet been
widely used or audited. The API may change, and edge cases may exist. If
you need a mature, battle-tested YAML library, consider `serde_yml` or
`serde-yaml-ng` instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#why-libfyaml)Why libfyaml?

`fyaml` is built on [libfyaml](https://github.com/pantoniou/libfyaml), a
modern C library that offers several advantages over the traditional
`libyaml`:

- **Full YAML 1.2 compliance**with YAML 1.3 preparation
- **Zero-copy architecture**for efficient large document handling
- **No artificial limits**(libyaml has a- [1024-char implicit key limit](https://github.com/yaml/libyaml/blob/master/src/scanner.c#L1065-L1074))
- [Up to 24x faster](https://github.com/pantoniou/libfyaml/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md#091---2025-12-28)
- **Rich manipulation APIs**including YPATH expressions for path queries
- **MIT licensed**(as of v0.9.1)

This makes `fyaml` suitable for use cases requiring DOM manipulation,
YAML transformation tools, or configuration inspection utilities where
path-based queries are convenient.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- Parse YAML strings into document objects
- **Zero-copy scalar access**via lifetime-bound- `NodeRef`and- `ValueRef`
- Navigate nodes using path-based queries (e.g., `/foo/bar`,`/list/0`)
- Support for all YAML node types: scalars, sequences, and mappings
- Iterate over mapping key-value pairs and sequence items
- Convert nodes back to YAML strings
- Multi-document stream parsing via `FyParser`
- Read YAML from stdin (single document or stream)
- **Document mutation**via- `Editor`with compile-time safety
- **Style and comment preservation**during edits: comments, quote styles, block/flow structure
- `ValueRef`type- `as_str()`,- `as_bool()`,- `as_i64()`,- `as_f64()`,- `is_null()`
- Non-plain scalars (quoted, literal, folded) preserved as strings

- `Value`type- Serialize/deserialize with any serde-compatible format (JSON, TOML, etc.)
- Emit YAML using libfyaml for standards-compliant output
- Convenient indexing: `value["key"]`,`value[0]`

[§](https://docs.rs#error-handling)Error Handling

Parse errors include detailed location information (line and column numbers), making it easy to report errors to users or integrate with IDEs and linters.

```
use fyaml::Document;
let result = Document::parse_str("[unclosed bracket");
if let Err(e) = result {
    // Access structured error info
    if let fyaml::Error::ParseError(parse_err) = &e {
        println!("Error: {}", parse_err.message());
        if let Some((line, col)) = parse_err.location() {
            println!("At line {}, column {}", line, col);
        }
    }
    // Or just display it nicely
    println!("{}", e);  // "Parse error at 2:1: flow sequence without a closing bracket"
}
```
The `ParseError` type provides:

- `message()`- The error message from libfyaml
- `line()`- Line number (1-based), if available
- `column()`- Column number (1-based), if available
- `location()`- Tuple of (line, column) if both available

All parsing methods (`Document::parse_str`, `Document::from_string`,
`Document::from_bytes`, `Editor::build_from_yaml`) capture errors
silently without printing to stderr, making the library suitable for use
in GUI applications and test suites.

[§](https://docs.rs#zero-copy-architecture)Zero-Copy Architecture

`fyaml` leverages libfyaml’s zero-copy design for efficient memory
usage. When you access scalar values through `NodeRef` or `ValueRef`,
you get references directly into the parsed document buffer - no string
copying or allocation occurs.

```
use fyaml::Document;
let doc = Document::parse_str("message: Hello, World!").unwrap();
let root = doc.root().unwrap();
let node = root.at_path("/message").unwrap();
// Zero-copy: this &str points directly into the document's memory
let s: &str = node.scalar_str().unwrap();
assert_eq!(s, "Hello, World!");
// The reference is tied to the document's lifetime -
// this prevents use-after-free at compile time
```
This is particularly beneficial for:

- **Large documents**: Read gigabytes of YAML without doubling memory usage
- **Config parsing**: Extract only the values you need without copying everything
- **High-throughput processing**: Minimize allocations in hot paths

[§](https://docs.rs#style-and-comment-preservation)Style and Comment Preservation

When modifying documents with `Editor`, `fyaml` preserves formatting and
comments. This is essential for configuration files where maintaining
the original style improves readability and diff-friendliness.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-preserved)What IS preserved:

- **Comments**: Top-level, inline, and end-of-line comments
- **Quote styles**: Single-quoted (- `'value'`), double-quoted (- `"value"`), and plain scalars
- **Block scalar styles**: Literal (- `|`) and folded (- `>`) blocks
- **Collection styles**: Flow (- `[a, b]`,- `{a: 1}`) vs block (indented) sequences/mappings

```
use fyaml::Document;
// Comments and quote styles are preserved through edits
let yaml = "# Database configuration
database:
  host: 'localhost'  # local dev server
  port: 5432
";
let mut doc = Document::parse_str(yaml).unwrap();
{
    let mut ed = doc.edit();
    ed.set_yaml_at("/database/port", "5433").unwrap();
}
let output = doc.emit().unwrap();
// Comments preserved
assert!(output.contains("# Database configuration"));
assert!(output.contains("# local dev server"));
// Quote style preserved
assert!(output.contains("'localhost'"));
```
Block scalars are also preserved:

```
use fyaml::Document;
let yaml = "script: |
  echo hello
  echo world
name: test
";
let mut doc = Document::parse_str(yaml).unwrap();
{
    let mut ed = doc.edit();
    ed.set_yaml_at("/name", "modified").unwrap();
}
let output = doc.emit().unwrap();
// Literal block style (|) is preserved for the script
assert!(output.contains("script: |"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-notes)Formatting notes:

- Flow collections (`[a, b]`,`{a: 1}`) are preserved as flow style but may be reformatted across multiple lines by libfyaml’s emitter

[§](https://docs.rs#path-syntax)Path Syntax

Paths use `/` as the separator (YPATH/JSON Pointer style):

- `/key`- access a mapping key
- `/0`- access a sequence index
- `/parent/child/0`- nested access

```
use fyaml::Document;
let yaml = "
database:
  host: localhost
  ports:
    - 5432
    - 5433
";
let doc = Document::parse_str(yaml).unwrap();
let root = doc.root().unwrap();
// Access mapping key
let db = root.at_path("/database").unwrap();
assert!(db.is_mapping());
// Nested access
let host = root.at_path("/database/host").unwrap();
assert_eq!(host.scalar_str().unwrap(), "localhost");
// Sequence index
let first_port = root.at_path("/database/ports/0").unwrap();
assert_eq!(first_port.scalar_str().unwrap(), "5432");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#working-with-value-high-level-owned)Working with Value (high-level, owned)

The `Value` type provides a convenient, serde-compatible way to work
with YAML:

```
use fyaml::Value;
// Parse YAML
let value: Value = "name: Alice\nage: 30".parse().unwrap();
// Access values with indexing
assert_eq!(value["name"].as_str(), Some("Alice"));
assert_eq!(value["age"].as_i64(), Some(30));
// Emit back to YAML
let yaml = value.to_yaml_string().unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#zero-copy-with-document-and-noderef)Zero-copy with Document and NodeRef

For more control and zero-copy scalar access, use the `Document` API:

```
use fyaml::Document;
let doc = Document::parse_str("database:\n  host: localhost\n  port: 5432").unwrap();
let root = doc.root().unwrap();
// Zero-copy: returns &str pointing into document memory
let host = root.at_path("/database/host").unwrap();
assert_eq!(host.scalar_str().unwrap(), "localhost");
// Navigation by path
let port = root.at_path("/database/port").unwrap();
assert_eq!(port.scalar_str().unwrap(), "5432");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#zero-copy-typed-access-with-valueref)Zero-copy typed access with ValueRef

`ValueRef` wraps `NodeRef` and provides typed accessors that interpret
YAML scalars on demand without allocation:

```
use fyaml::Document;
let doc = Document::parse_str("name: Alice\nage: 30\nactive: yes").unwrap();
let root = doc.root_value().unwrap();
// Zero-copy typed access
assert_eq!(root.get("name").unwrap().as_str(), Some("Alice"));
assert_eq!(root.get("age").unwrap().as_i64(), Some(30));
assert_eq!(root.get("active").unwrap().as_bool(), Some(true));  // yes -> true
```
Non-plain scalars (quoted, literal `|`, folded `>`) are NOT
type-interpreted:

```
use fyaml::Document;
let doc = Document::parse_str("quoted: 'true'\nunquoted: true").unwrap();
let root = doc.root_value().unwrap();
// Quoted: string, not bool
assert_eq!(root.get("quoted").unwrap().as_bool(), None);
assert_eq!(root.get("quoted").unwrap().as_str(), Some("true"));
// Unquoted: interpreted as bool
assert_eq!(root.get("unquoted").unwrap().as_bool(), Some(true));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#mutation-with-editor)Mutation with Editor

Use `Document::edit()` to get an exclusive `Editor` for modifications:

```
use fyaml::Document;
let mut doc = Document::parse_str("name: Alice").unwrap();
// Mutation phase - NodeRef cannot exist during this
{
    let mut ed = doc.edit();
    ed.set_yaml_at("/name", "'Bob'").unwrap();   // Preserve quotes
    ed.set_yaml_at("/age", "30").unwrap();       // Add new key
    ed.delete_at("/name").unwrap();              // Delete key
    ed.set_yaml_at("/name", "\"Charlie\"").unwrap();  // Re-add
}
// Read phase - safe to access nodes again
let root = doc.root().unwrap();
assert_eq!(root.at_path("/name").unwrap().scalar_str().unwrap(), "Charlie");
assert_eq!(root.at_path("/age").unwrap().scalar_str().unwrap(), "30");
```
Building complex structures:

```
use fyaml::Document;
let mut doc = Document::new().unwrap();
{
    let mut ed = doc.edit();
    let root = ed.build_from_yaml("users:\n  - name: Alice\n  - name: Bob").unwrap();
    ed.set_root(root).unwrap();
}
assert!(doc.root().is_some());
```
Modifying sequence elements:

```
use fyaml::Document;
let mut doc = Document::parse_str("items:\n  - a\n  - b\n  - c").unwrap();
{
    let mut ed = doc.edit();
    // Replace by positive index
    ed.set_yaml_at("/items/0", "first").unwrap();
    // Replace by negative index (Python-style: -1 = last element)
    ed.set_yaml_at("/items/-1", "last").unwrap();
}
assert_eq!(doc.at_path("/items/0").unwrap().scalar_str().unwrap(), "first");
assert_eq!(doc.at_path("/items/1").unwrap().scalar_str().unwrap(), "b");
assert_eq!(doc.at_path("/items/2").unwrap().scalar_str().unwrap(), "last");
```
Building structures programmatically with handle-level operations:

```
use fyaml::Document;
let mut doc = Document::new().unwrap();
{
    let mut ed = doc.edit();
    // Build a sequence of servers
    let mut servers = ed.build_sequence().unwrap();
    let s1 = ed.build_scalar("web1").unwrap();
    let s2 = ed.build_scalar("web2").unwrap();
    ed.seq_append(&mut servers, s1).unwrap();
    ed.seq_append(&mut servers, s2).unwrap();
    // Build the root mapping
    let mut root = ed.build_mapping().unwrap();
    let k1 = ed.build_scalar("host").unwrap();
    let v1 = ed.build_scalar("localhost").unwrap();
    ed.map_insert(&mut root, k1, v1).unwrap();
    let k2 = ed.build_scalar("port").unwrap();
    let v2 = ed.build_null().unwrap();
    ed.map_insert(&mut root, k2, v2).unwrap();
    let k3 = ed.build_scalar("servers").unwrap();
    ed.map_insert(&mut root, k3, servers).unwrap();
    // Tag the root
    ed.set_tag(&mut root, "!config").unwrap();
    ed.set_root(root).unwrap();
}
let root = doc.root().unwrap();
assert_eq!(root.at_path("/host").unwrap().scalar_str().unwrap(), "localhost");
assert_eq!(root.tag_str().unwrap().unwrap(), "!config");
assert_eq!(root.at_path("/servers/0").unwrap().scalar_str().unwrap(), "web1");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#multi-document-parsing-with-fyparser)Multi-document parsing with FyParser

Use `FyParser` for parsing YAML streams with multiple documents:

```
use fyaml::FyParser;
let yaml = "---\ndoc1: value1\n---\ndoc2: value2";
let parser = FyParser::from_string(yaml).unwrap();
let docs: Vec<_> = parser.doc_iter().filter_map(|r| r.ok()).collect();
assert_eq!(docs.len(), 2);
// Each document is independent
assert_eq!(docs[0].at_path("/doc1").unwrap().scalar_str().unwrap(), "value1");
assert_eq!(docs[1].at_path("/doc2").unwrap().scalar_str().unwrap(), "value2");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#reading-from-stdin)Reading from stdin

For CLI tools that read YAML from stdin:

```
use fyaml::Document;
// Single document from stdin
let doc = Document::from_stdin().unwrap();
println!("{}", doc.emit().unwrap());
```
For multi-document streams:

```
use fyaml::FyParser;
// Default: line-buffered mode for interactive/streaming use
let parser = FyParser::from_stdin().unwrap();
for doc_result in parser.doc_iter() {
    let doc = doc_result.unwrap();
    println!("{}", doc.emit().unwrap());
}
```
For batch processing where efficiency matters more than interactivity:

```
use fyaml::FyParser;
// Block-buffered mode: more efficient for large inputs
let parser = FyParser::from_stdin_with_line_buffer(false).unwrap();
for doc_result in parser.doc_iter() {
    // Process each document
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#serde-integration)Serde integration

`Value` works with any serde-compatible format:

```
use fyaml::Value;
let value: Value = "key: value".parse().unwrap();
// Convert to JSON
let json = serde_json::to_string(&value).unwrap();
assert_eq!(json, r#"{"key":"value"}"#);
// Parse from JSON
let from_json: Value = serde_json::from_str(&json).unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#iterating-over-mappings)Iterating over mappings

```
use fyaml::Document;
let doc = Document::parse_str("a: 1\nb: 2\nc: 3").unwrap();
let root = doc.root().unwrap();
for (key, value) in root.map_iter() {
    println!("{}: {}", key.scalar_str().unwrap(), value.scalar_str().unwrap());
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#iterating-over-sequences)Iterating over sequences

```
use fyaml::Document;
let doc = Document::parse_str("- apple\n- banana\n- cherry").unwrap();
let root = doc.root().unwrap();
for item in root.seq_iter() {
    println!("{}", item.scalar_str().unwrap());
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#checking-node-types)Checking node types

```
use fyaml::{Document, NodeType};
let doc = Document::parse_str("key: value").unwrap();
let root = doc.root().unwrap();
assert!(root.is_mapping());
assert_eq!(root.kind(), NodeType::Mapping);
let value = root.at_path("/key").unwrap();
assert!(value.is_scalar());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#api-reference)API Reference

[§](https://docs.rs#main-types)Main Types

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| `Document` | Parsed YAML document (owns the data) |
| `NodeRef<'doc>` | Zero-copy reference to a node (borrows document) |
| `ValueRef<'doc>` | Zero-copy typed access (wraps NodeRef) |
| `Editor<'doc>` | Exclusive mutable access to document |
| `FyParser` | Multi-document stream parser |
| `Value` | Owned serde-compatible YAML value |
| `Number` | Numeric value: `Int(i64)`,`UInt(u64)`,`Float(f64)` |
| `TaggedValue` | Value with an associated YAML tag |
| `ParseError` | Rich parse error with line/column location |

[§](https://docs.rs#enums)Enums

| Type | Variants |
|---|---|
| `NodeType` | `Scalar`,`Sequence`,`Mapping` |
| `NodeStyle` | `Plain`,`SingleQuoted`,`DoubleQuoted`,`Literal`,`Folded`,
etc. |

[§](https://docs.rs#document-methods)Document Methods

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `Document::parse_str(yaml)` | Parse YAML string into Document |
| `Document::new()` | Create empty document |
| `Document::from_stdin()` | Parse single document from stdin |
| `doc.root()` | Get root node as `Option<NodeRef>` |
| `doc.root_value()` | Get root node as `Option<ValueRef>` |
| `doc.at_path(path)` | Navigate to node by path |
| `doc.edit()` | Get exclusive `Editor`for mutations |
| `doc.emit()` | Emit document as YAML string |

[§](https://docs.rs#choosing-a-library)Choosing a Library

-
**For serde integration**:`fyaml`provides a serde-compatible`Value`type with libfyaml-powered parsing and emission. Alternatives include`serde_yml`or`serde-yaml-ng`(based on unsafe-libyaml).
-
**For pure Rust**: Use`saphyr`or`yaml-rust2`(no C dependencies, easier to audit).
-
**For DOM manipulation and path queries**:`fyaml`provides convenient path-based navigation (`/foo/0/bar`) via libfyaml’s YPATH support, plus a`Value`type for programmatic manipulation.
-
**For maximum performance on large files**:`fyaml`benefits from libfyaml’s zero-copy architecture and streaming optimizations.

[§](https://docs.rs#changelog)Changelog

[§](https://docs.rs#052-2026-07-02)0.5.2 (2026-07-02)

[§](https://docs.rs#fix)Fix

-
Force infinite emit width to work around `libfyaml`scalar wrap corruption. [Valentin Lab]`libfyaml`’s emitter wraps lines at the configured width (default 80) by inserting a trailing`\`line-continuation. That escape is only valid in double-quoted style: in single-quoted (and plain) scalars the`\`is literal, so emitted YAML no longer round-trips (re-parsing yields a spurious`\`+ folded space).Bug present in upstream v1.0.0-alpha7 and master. Work around it with `FYECF_WIDTH_INF`in`emit_flags()`— the same workaround`fy-tool`itself applies when stdout is not a tty. Guarded by the new`emit_long_single_quoted_scalar_round_trips`regression test; drop the flag once upstream wrapping round-trips correctly.

[§](https://docs.rs#051-2026-06-26)0.5.1 (2026-06-26)

[§](https://docs.rs#fix-1)Fix

-
Upgrade to `fyaml-sys`0.1.1-alpha.2 (libfyaml v1.0.0-alpha7) [Valentin Lab]Bump the `fyaml-sys`dependency to`=0.1.1-alpha.2`, which vendors libfyaml`v1.0.0-alpha7`. This fixes a re-emit bug where a block literal/folded scalar followed by a comment had the comment fused onto the scalar’s last content line (e.g.`fi## comment`).libfyaml v1.0 renamed the parse-config flag `FYPCF_PARSE_COMMENTS`to`FYPCF_KEEP_COMMENTS`(keeping the old name only as a`#define`alias, which bindgen does not surface). Update`config.rs`accordingly.Add a regression test asserting a block scalar followed by a comment no longer fuses the comment into the scalar on a parse -> emit round-trip.

[§](https://docs.rs#050-2026-02-02)0.5.0 (2026-02-02)

[§](https://docs.rs#new)New

-
Add `set_style`method to`Editor`[Valentin Lab]Allows setting the YAML style (plain, single-quoted, double-quoted, literal, folded, flow, block) on detached node handles. libfyaml validates the requested style against node content and may keep the current style if the request is invalid; the actually-applied style is returned.
-
Add handle-level `Editor`methods for programmatic node assembly. [Valentin Lab]Add `seq_append()`,`map_insert()`,`set_tag()`, and`build_null()`to`Editor`for building YAML structures without parsing YAML snippets. These complement the existing path-based API (`set_yaml_at`,`seq_append_at`) with lower-level handle operations.Update `README.org`with API table entries and a usage example.

[§](https://docs.rs#fix-2)Fix

-
Quote ambiguous strings during `Value`YAML emission. [Valentin Lab]Strings like “true”, “null”, “42” were emitted as plain scalars, causing them to be reinterpreted as bool/null/number on re-parse. Now `needs_quoting()`detects such values and the emitter wraps them in single quotes so they roundtrip correctly as`Value::String`.
-
`build_null()`now produces a proper YAML null node. [Valentin Lab]`fy_node_create_scalar_copy(doc, NULL, 0)`creates an empty scalar without libfyaml’s internal`is_null`flag, making it indistinguishable from`build_scalar("")`. Switch to`build_from_yaml("null")`which goes through the parser and sets`is_null = true`.Tighten null emission tests: `Value::Null`must emit exactly`"null"`, and must differ from`Value::String("")`.
-
`Value::to_yaml_string()`no longer adds trailing newline. [Valentin Lab]`to_yaml_string()`was using document-level emission (`fy_emit_document_to_string`) which appends`\n`. Rewrite to use node-level emission via`Editor`API, matching`NodeRef::emit()`behavior.Tighten existing test assertions that masked this with `.trim()`.

[§](https://docs.rs#040-2026-01-24)0.4.0 (2026-01-24)

- Validate index bounds and return error for out-of-bounds access
- Update documentation with sequence examples and supported parent types
- Add comprehensive tests for sequence manipulation edge cases

[§](https://docs.rs#030-2026-01-22)0.3.0 (2026-01-22)

- Add `diag`module to capture libfyaml errors via`fy_diag`callbacks

- Update `Document::parse_str`,`from_string`,`from_bytes`to return`Error::ParseError`with location info

 This makes the library suitable for GUI applications and IDEs that need structured error information without stderr pollution.

[§](https://docs.rs#020-2026-01-20)0.2.0 (2026-01-20)

[§](https://docs.rs#new-3)New

-
Add `from_stdin_with_line_buffer()`for configurable stdin buffering. [Valentin Lab]Allows callers to control whether stdin uses line-buffered or block-buffered mode. Line-buffered is useful for streaming/interactive use (process documents as lines arrive), while block-buffered is more efficient for batch processing. The existing `from_stdin()`method now delegates to this with line_buffered=true to preserve backward compatibility.

# Cream

Cream is a compiler that enables you to write frontend user interfaces with declarative code and compiles to HTML. It offers a modern approach to building web applications, with features designed to enhance productivity and performance.

## Introduction

Cream simplifies frontend development by providing a straightforward way to write UI code using a declarative syntax. With Cream, you can create reactive user interfaces with minimal overhead, resulting in faster development cycles and more maintainable code.

## Features

-
**Compiled JavaScript with Zero Abstraction**: Cream generates JavaScript code without introducing unnecessary abstractions, resulting in efficient and maintainable code.
-
**Reactive States Without Weird APIs**: Cream provides reactive state management without relying on complex or unfamiliar APIs, making it easy to manage application state.
-
**Standard Library**: Cream includes a standard library with functions for tasks such as fetching data, error handling, data extraction, hashing, and cycling data, streamlining common development tasks.
-
**Build Full-Stack Web Apps**: Cream can be used to build full-stack web applications in conjunction with any backend framework, offering flexibility and interoperability.
-
**No**: Cream does not rely on`node_modules`Required`node_modules`for its functionality, eliminating unnecessary dependencies and simplifying project setup. This is particularly beneficial for projects that do not use TypeScript or Tailwind CSS.
-
**No Bundler Required**: Cream eliminates the need for bundlers, enabling simpler and more efficient build processes.
-
**Native Typescript**: Cream eliminates the need for any explicit runtime or the typescipt compiler to write typescript scripts for your web app.

## Installation

To install the latest version of cream on macOS or Linux, run the following command in your terminal:

```
```
For detailed documentation and usage examples, visit [cream](https://tm-ahad.github.io/cream_docs).

# signal_hook_registry - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/signal-hook-registry/1.4.8/target-redirect/signal_hook_registry/

## Expand description

Backend of the [signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) crate.

The [signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) crate tries to provide an API to the unix signals, which are a global
resource. Therefore, it is desirable an application contains just one version of the crate
which manages this global resource. But that makes it impossible to make breaking changes in
the API.

Therefore, this crate provides very minimal and low level API to the signals that is unlikely
to have to change, while there may be multiple versions of the [signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) that all use this
low-level API to provide different versions of the high level APIs.

It is also possible some other crates might want to build a completely different API. This split allows these crates to still reuse the same low-level routines in this crate instead of going to the (much more dangerous) unix calls.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-this-crate-provides)What this crate provides

The only thing this crate does is multiplexing the signals. An application or library can add or remove callbacks and have multiple callbacks for the same signal.

It handles dispatching the callbacks and managing them in a way that uses only the
[async-signal-safe](http://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal-safety.7.html) functions inside the signal handler. Note that the callbacks are still run
inside the signal handler, so it is up to the caller to ensure they are also
[async-signal-safe](http://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal-safety.7.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#what-this-is-for)What this is for

This is a building block for other libraries creating reasonable abstractions on top of
signals. The [signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) is the generally preferred way if you need to handle signals in your
application and provides several safe patterns of doing so.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version-compatibility)Rust version compatibility

Currently builds on 1.26.0 an newer and this is very unlikely to change. However, tests require dependencies that don’t build there, so tests need newer Rust version (they are run on stable).

Note that this ancient version of rustc no longer compiles current versions of `libc`. If you
want to use rustc this old, you need to force your dependency resolution to pick old enough
version of `libc` (`0.2.156` was found to work, but newer ones may too).

[§](https://docs.rs#portability)Portability

This crate includes a limited support for Windows, based on `signal`/`raise` in the CRT.
There are differences in both API and behavior:

- Due to lack of `siginfo_t`, we don’t provide`register_sigaction`or`register_unchecked`.
- Due to lack of signal blocking, there’s a race condition.
After the call to `signal`, there’s a moment where we miss a signal. That means when you register a handler, there may be a signal which invokes neither the default handler or the handler you register.
- Handlers registered by `signal`in Windows are cleared on first signal. To match behavior in other platforms, we re-register the handler each time the handler is called, but there’s a moment where we miss a handler. That means when you receive two signals in a row, there may be a signal which invokes the default handler, nevertheless you certainly have registered the handler.

# signal_hook_registry - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/signal-hook-registry/1.4.8/signal_hook_registry/index.html

## Expand description

Backend of the [signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) crate.

The [signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) crate tries to provide an API to the unix signals, which are a global
resource. Therefore, it is desirable an application contains just one version of the crate
which manages this global resource. But that makes it impossible to make breaking changes in
the API.

Therefore, this crate provides very minimal and low level API to the signals that is unlikely
to have to change, while there may be multiple versions of the [signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) that all use this
low-level API to provide different versions of the high level APIs.

It is also possible some other crates might want to build a completely different API. This split allows these crates to still reuse the same low-level routines in this crate instead of going to the (much more dangerous) unix calls.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-this-crate-provides)What this crate provides

The only thing this crate does is multiplexing the signals. An application or library can add or remove callbacks and have multiple callbacks for the same signal.

It handles dispatching the callbacks and managing them in a way that uses only the
[async-signal-safe](http://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal-safety.7.html) functions inside the signal handler. Note that the callbacks are still run
inside the signal handler, so it is up to the caller to ensure they are also
[async-signal-safe](http://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal-safety.7.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#what-this-is-for)What this is for

This is a building block for other libraries creating reasonable abstractions on top of
signals. The [signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) is the generally preferred way if you need to handle signals in your
application and provides several safe patterns of doing so.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version-compatibility)Rust version compatibility

Currently builds on 1.26.0 an newer and this is very unlikely to change. However, tests require dependencies that don’t build there, so tests need newer Rust version (they are run on stable).

Note that this ancient version of rustc no longer compiles current versions of `libc`. If you
want to use rustc this old, you need to force your dependency resolution to pick old enough
version of `libc` (`0.2.156` was found to work, but newer ones may too).

[§](https://docs.rs#portability)Portability

This crate includes a limited support for Windows, based on `signal`/`raise` in the CRT.
There are differences in both API and behavior:

- Due to lack of `siginfo_t`, we don’t provide`register_sigaction`or`register_unchecked`.
- Due to lack of signal blocking, there’s a race condition.
After the call to `signal`, there’s a moment where we miss a signal. That means when you register a handler, there may be a signal which invokes neither the default handler or the handler you register.
- Handlers registered by `signal`in Windows are cleared on first signal. To match behavior in other platforms, we re-register the handler each time the handler is called, but there’s a moment where we miss a handler. That means when you receive two signals in a row, there may be a signal which invokes the default handler, nevertheless you certainly have registered the handler.

[111](https://docs.rs#111)// # Internal workings
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//
[113](https://docs.rs#113)// This uses a form of RCU. There's an atomic pointer to the current action descriptors (in the
[114](https://docs.rs#114)// form of IndependentArcSwap, to be able to track what, if any, signal handlers still use the
[115](https://docs.rs#115)// version). A signal handler takes a copy of the pointer and calls all the relevant actions.
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//
[117](https://docs.rs#117)// Modifications to that are protected by a mutex, to avoid juggling multiple signal handlers at
[118](https://docs.rs#118)// once (eg. not calling sigaction concurrently). This should not be a problem, because modifying
[119](https://docs.rs#119)// the signal actions should be initialization only anyway. To avoid all allocations and also
[120](https://docs.rs#120)// deallocations inside the signal handler, after replacing the pointer, the modification routine
[121](https://docs.rs#121)// needs to busy-wait for the reference count on the old pointer to drop to 1 and take ownership ‒
[122](https://docs.rs#122)// that way the one deallocating is the modification routine, outside of the signal handler.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)
[124](https://docs.rs#124)#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, Ord, PartialOrd, Hash)]

[164](https://docs.rs#164)        // C data structure, expected to be zeroed out.
[165](https://docs.rs#165)        let mut new: libc::sigaction = unsafe { mem::zeroed() };
[166](https://docs.rs#166)
[167](https://docs.rs#167)        // Note: AIX fixed their naming in libc 0.2.171.
[168](https://docs.rs#168)        //
[169](https://docs.rs#169)        // However, if we mandate that _for everyone_, other systems fail to compile on old Rust
[170](https://docs.rs#170)        // versions (eg. 1.26.0), because they are no longer able to compile this new libc.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)        //

[173](https://docs.rs#173)        // (it doesn't compile the ones it doesn't need, but it stills considers the other targets
[174](https://docs.rs#174)        // for version resolution).
[175](https://docs.rs#175)        //
[176](https://docs.rs#176)        // Therefore, we let the user have freedom - if they want AIX, they can upgrade to new
[177](https://docs.rs#177)        // enough libc. If they want ancient rustc, they can force older versions of libc.
[178](https://docs.rs#178)        //
[179](https://docs.rs#179)        // See #169.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)
[181](https://docs.rs#181)        new.sa_sigaction = handler as *const () as usize; // If it doesn't compile on AIX, upgrade the libc dependency
[182](https://docs.rs#182)
[183](https://docs.rs#183)        #[cfg(target_os = "nto")]
[184](https://docs.rs#184)        let flags = 0;
[185](https://docs.rs#185)        // SA_RESTART is not supported by qnx https://www.qnx.com/support/knowledgebase.html?id=50130000000SmiD
[186](https://docs.rs#186)        #[cfg(not(target_os = "nto"))]
[187](https://docs.rs#187)        let flags = libc::SA_RESTART;
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        // Android is broken and uses different int types than the rest (and different depending on
[189](https://docs.rs#189)        // the pointer width). This converts the flags to the proper type no matter what it is on
[190](https://docs.rs#190)        // the given platform.
[191](https://docs.rs#191)        #[allow(unused_assignments)]

[193](https://docs.rs#193)        siginfo = libc::SA_SIGINFO as _;
[194](https://docs.rs#194)        let flags = flags | siginfo;
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        new.sa_flags = flags as _;
[196](https://docs.rs#196)        // C data structure, expected to be zeroed out.
[197](https://docs.rs#197)        let mut old: libc::sigaction = unsafe { mem::zeroed() };
[198](https://docs.rs#198)        // FFI ‒ pointers are valid, it doesn't take ownership.
[199](https://docs.rs#199)        if unsafe { libc::sigaction(signal, &new, &mut old) } != 0 {
[200](https://docs.rs#200)            return Err(Error::last_os_error());
[201](https://docs.rs#201)        }
[202](https://docs.rs#202)        Ok(Slot {
[203](https://docs.rs#203)            prev: Prev { signal, info: old },

[205](https://docs.rs#205)        })

[247](https://docs.rs#247)    fn execute(&self, sig: c_int) {
[248](https://docs.rs#248)        let fptr = self.info;
[249](https://docs.rs#249)        if fptr != 0 && fptr != SIG_DFL && fptr != SIG_IGN {
[250](https://docs.rs#250)            // `sighandler_t` is an integer type. Transmuting it directly from an integer to a
[251](https://docs.rs#251)            // function pointer seems dubious w.r.t. pointer provenance -- at least Miri complains
[252](https://docs.rs#252)            // about it. Casting to a raw pointer first side-steps the issue.
[253](https://docs.rs#253)            let fptr = fptr as *mut ();
[254](https://docs.rs#254)            // FFI ‒ calling the original signal handler.
[255](https://docs.rs#255)            unsafe {
[256](https://docs.rs#256)                let action = mem::transmute::<*mut (), extern "C" fn(c_int)>(fptr);
[257](https://docs.rs#257)                action(sig);
[258](https://docs.rs#258)            }
[259](https://docs.rs#259)        }
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    #[cfg(not(windows))]
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    // libc re-exports the core::ffi::c_void on rustc >= 1.30, else defines its own type
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    // cfg_attr is needed because the `allow(clippy::lint)` syntax was added in Rust 1.31
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    #[cfg_attr(clippy, allow(clippy::incompatible_msrv))]
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    unsafe fn execute(&self, sig: c_int, info: *mut siginfo_t, data: *mut c_void) {
[267](https://docs.rs#267)        let fptr = self.info.sa_sigaction;
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        if fptr != 0 && fptr != libc::SIG_DFL && fptr != libc::SIG_IGN {
[269](https://docs.rs#269)            // `sa_sigaction` is usually stored as integer type. Transmuting it directly from an
[270](https://docs.rs#270)            // integer to a function pointer seems dubious w.r.t. pointer provenance -- at least
[271](https://docs.rs#271)            // Miri complains about it. Casting to a raw pointer first side-steps the issue.
[272](https://docs.rs#272)            let fptr = fptr as *mut ();
[273](https://docs.rs#273)            // Android is broken and uses different int types than the rest (and different
[274](https://docs.rs#274)            // depending on the pointer width). This converts the flags to the proper type no
[275](https://docs.rs#275)            // matter what it is on the given platform.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)            //
[277](https://docs.rs#277)            // The trick is to create the same-typed variable as the sa_flags first and then
[278](https://docs.rs#278)            // set it to the proper value (does Rust have a way to copy a type in a different
[279](https://docs.rs#279)            // way?)
[280](https://docs.rs#280)            #[allow(unused_assignments)]
[281](https://docs.rs#281)            let mut siginfo = self.info.sa_flags;
[282](https://docs.rs#282)            siginfo = libc::SA_SIGINFO as _;
[283](https://docs.rs#283)            if self.info.sa_flags & siginfo == 0 {
[284](https://docs.rs#284)                let action = mem::transmute::<*mut (), extern "C" fn(c_int)>(fptr);
[285](https://docs.rs#285)                action(sig);
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            } else {
[287](https://docs.rs#287)                type SigAction = extern "C" fn(c_int, *mut siginfo_t, *mut c_void);
[288](https://docs.rs#288)                let action = mem::transmute::<*mut (), SigAction>(fptr);
[289](https://docs.rs#289)                action(sig, info, data);
[290](https://docs.rs#290)            }
[291](https://docs.rs#291)        }
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    }
[293](https://docs.rs#293)}
[294](https://docs.rs#294)
[295](https://docs.rs#295)/// Lazy-initiated data structure with our global variables.
[296](https://docs.rs#296)///
[297](https://docs.rs#297)/// Used inside a structure to cut down on boilerplate code to lazy-initialize stuff. We don't dare
[298](https://docs.rs#298)/// use anything fancy like lazy-static or once-cell, since we are not sure they are
[299](https://docs.rs#299)/// async-signal-safe in their access. Our code uses the [Once], but only on the write end outside
[300](https://docs.rs#300)/// of signal handler. The handler assumes it has already been initialized.
[301](https://docs.rs#301)struct GlobalData {
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    /// The data structure describing what needs to be run for each signal.
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    data: HalfLock<SignalData>,
[304](https://docs.rs#304)
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    /// A fallback to fight/minimize a race condition during signal initialization.
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    ///
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    /// See the comment inside [`register_unchecked_impl`].
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    race_fallback: HalfLock<Option<Prev>>,
[309](https://docs.rs#309)}
[310](https://docs.rs#310)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)static GLOBAL_DATA: AtomicPtr<GlobalData> = AtomicPtr::new(ptr::null_mut());
[312](https://docs.rs#312)#[allow(deprecated)]
[313](https://docs.rs#313)static GLOBAL_INIT: Once = ONCE_INIT;
[314](https://docs.rs#314)
[315](https://docs.rs#315)impl GlobalData {
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    fn get() -> &'static Self {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)        let data = GLOBAL_DATA.load(Ordering::Acquire);
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        // # Safety
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        //
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        // * The data actually does live forever - created by Box::into_raw.
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        // * It is _never_ modified (apart for interior mutability, but that one is fine).
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        unsafe { data.as_ref().expect("We shall be set up already") }
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    }
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    fn ensure() -> &'static Self {
[325](https://docs.rs#325)        GLOBAL_INIT.call_once(|| {
[326](https://docs.rs#326)            let data = Box::into_raw(Box::new(GlobalData {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)                data: HalfLock::new(SignalData {
[328](https://docs.rs#328)                    signals: VecMap::new(),
[329](https://docs.rs#329)                    next_id: 1,
[330](https://docs.rs#330)                }),
[331](https://docs.rs#331)                race_fallback: HalfLock::new(None),
[332](https://docs.rs#332)            }));
[333](https://docs.rs#333)            let old = GLOBAL_DATA.swap(data, Ordering::Release);
[334](https://docs.rs#334)            assert!(old.is_null());
[335](https://docs.rs#335)        });
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        Self::get()
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    }
[338](https://docs.rs#338)}
[339](https://docs.rs#339)
[340](https://docs.rs#340)#[cfg(windows)]
[341](https://docs.rs#341)extern "C" fn handler(sig: c_int) {
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    let _errno = ErrnoGuard::new();
[343](https://docs.rs#343)
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    if sig != SIGFPE {
[345](https://docs.rs#345)        // Windows CRT `signal` resets handler every time, unless for SIGFPE.
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        // Reregister the handler to retain maximal compatibility.
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        // Problems:
[348](https://docs.rs#348)        // - It's racy. But this is inevitably racy in Windows.
[349](https://docs.rs#349)        // - Interacts poorly with handlers outside signal-hook-registry.
[350](https://docs.rs#350)        let old = unsafe { libc::signal(sig, handler as *const () as sighandler_t) };
[351](https://docs.rs#351)        if old == SIG_ERR {
[352](https://docs.rs#352)            // MSDN doesn't describe which errors might occur,
[353](https://docs.rs#353)            // but we can tell from the Linux manpage that
[354](https://docs.rs#354)            // EINVAL (invalid signal number) is mostly the only case.
[355](https://docs.rs#355)            // Therefore, this branch must not occur.
[356](https://docs.rs#356)            // In any case we can do nothing useful in the signal handler,
[357](https://docs.rs#357)            // so we're going to abort silently.
[358](https://docs.rs#358)            unsafe {
[359](https://docs.rs#359)                libc::abort();
[360](https://docs.rs#360)            }
[361](https://docs.rs#361)        }
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    }
[363](https://docs.rs#363)
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    let globals = GlobalData::get();
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    let fallback = globals.race_fallback.read();
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    let sigdata = globals.data.read();
[367](https://docs.rs#367)
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    if let Some(ref slot) = sigdata.signals.get(&sig) {
[369](https://docs.rs#369)        slot.prev.execute(sig);
[370](https://docs.rs#370)
[371](https://docs.rs#371)        for action in slot.actions.values() {
[372](https://docs.rs#372)            action(&siginfo_t);
[373](https://docs.rs#373)        }
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    } else if let Some(prev) = fallback.as_ref() {
[375](https://docs.rs#375)        // In case we get called but don't have the slot for this signal set up yet, we are under
[376](https://docs.rs#376)        // the race condition. We may have the old signal handler stored in the fallback
[377](https://docs.rs#377)        // temporarily.
[378](https://docs.rs#378)        if sig == prev.signal {
[379](https://docs.rs#379)            prev.execute(sig);
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        }
[381](https://docs.rs#381)        // else -> probably should not happen, but races with other threads are possible so
[382](https://docs.rs#382)        // better safe
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    }
[384](https://docs.rs#384)}
[385](https://docs.rs#385)
[386](https://docs.rs#386)#[cfg(not(windows))]
[387](https://docs.rs#387)// libc re-exports the core::ffi::c_void on rustc >= 1.30, else defines its own type
[388](https://docs.rs#388)// cfg_attr is needed because the `allow(clippy::lint)` syntax was added in Rust 1.31
[389](https://docs.rs#389)#[cfg_attr(clippy, allow(clippy::incompatible_msrv))]
[390](https://docs.rs#390)extern "C" fn handler(sig: c_int, info: *mut siginfo_t, data: *mut c_void) {
[391](https://docs.rs#391)    let _errno = ErrnoGuard::new();
[392](https://docs.rs#392)
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    let globals = GlobalData::get();
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    let fallback = globals.race_fallback.read();
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    let sigdata = globals.data.read();
[396](https://docs.rs#396)
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    if let Some(slot) = sigdata.signals.get(&sig) {
[398](https://docs.rs#398)        unsafe { slot.prev.execute(sig, info, data) };
[399](https://docs.rs#399)
[400](https://docs.rs#400)        let info = unsafe { info.as_ref() };
[401](https://docs.rs#401)        let info = info.unwrap_or_else(|| {
[402](https://docs.rs#402)            // The info being null seems to be illegal according to POSIX, but has been observed on
[403](https://docs.rs#403)            // some probably broken platform. We can't do anything about that, that is just broken,
[404](https://docs.rs#404)            // but we are not allowed to panic in a signal handler, so we are left only with simply
[405](https://docs.rs#405)            // aborting. We try to write a message what happens, but using the libc stuff
[406](https://docs.rs#406)            // (`eprintln` is not guaranteed to be async-signal-safe).
[407](https://docs.rs#407)            unsafe {
[408](https://docs.rs#408)                const MSG: &[u8] =
[409](https://docs.rs#409)                    b"Platform broken, got NULL as siginfo to signal handler. Aborting";
[410](https://docs.rs#410)                libc::write(2, MSG.as_ptr() as *const _, MSG.len());
[411](https://docs.rs#411)                libc::abort();
[412](https://docs.rs#412)            }
[413](https://docs.rs#413)        });
[414](https://docs.rs#414)
[415](https://docs.rs#415)        for action in slot.actions.values() {
[416](https://docs.rs#416)            action(info);
[417](https://docs.rs#417)        }
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    } else if let Some(prev) = fallback.as_ref() {
[419](https://docs.rs#419)        // In case we get called but don't have the slot for this signal set up yet, we are under
[420](https://docs.rs#420)        // the race condition. We may have the old signal handler stored in the fallback
[421](https://docs.rs#421)        // temporarily.
[422](https://docs.rs#422)        if prev.signal == sig {
[423](https://docs.rs#423)            unsafe { prev.execute(sig, info, data) };
[424](https://docs.rs#424)        }
[425](https://docs.rs#425)        // else -> probably should not happen, but races with other threads are possible so
[426](https://docs.rs#426)        // better safe
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    }

[443](https://docs.rs#443)
[444](https://docs.rs#444)/// List of forbidden signals.
[445](https://docs.rs#445)///
[446](https://docs.rs#446)/// Some signals are impossible to replace according to POSIX and some are so special that this
[447](https://docs.rs#447)/// library refuses to handle them (eg. SIGSEGV). The routines panic in case registering one of
[448](https://docs.rs#448)/// these signals is attempted.
[449](https://docs.rs#449)///
[450](https://docs.rs#450)/// See [`register`].
[451](https://docs.rs#451)pub const FORBIDDEN: &[c_int] = FORBIDDEN_IMPL;
[452](https://docs.rs#452)
[453](https://docs.rs#453)#[cfg(windows)]
[454](https://docs.rs#454)const FORBIDDEN_IMPL: &[c_int] = &[SIGILL, SIGFPE, SIGSEGV];
[455](https://docs.rs#455)#[cfg(not(windows))]
[456](https://docs.rs#456)const FORBIDDEN_IMPL: &[c_int] = &[SIGKILL, SIGSTOP, SIGILL, SIGFPE, SIGSEGV];
[457](https://docs.rs#457)
[458](https://docs.rs#458)/// Registers an arbitrary action for the given signal.
[459](https://docs.rs#459)///
[460](https://docs.rs#460)/// This makes sure there's a signal handler for the given signal. It then adds the action to the
[461](https://docs.rs#461)/// ones called each time the signal is delivered. If multiple actions are set for the same signal,
[462](https://docs.rs#462)/// all are called, in the order of registration.
[463](https://docs.rs#463)///
[464](https://docs.rs#464)/// If there was a previous signal handler for the given signal, it is chained ‒ it will be called
[465](https://docs.rs#465)/// as part of this library's signal handler, before any actions set through this function.
[466](https://docs.rs#466)///
[467](https://docs.rs#467)/// On success, the function returns an ID that can be used to remove the action again with
[468](https://docs.rs#468)/// [`unregister`].
[469](https://docs.rs#469)///
[470](https://docs.rs#470)/// # Panics
[471](https://docs.rs#471)///
[472](https://docs.rs#472)/// If the signal is one of (see [`FORBIDDEN`]):
[473](https://docs.rs#473)///
[474](https://docs.rs#474)/// * `SIGKILL`
[475](https://docs.rs#475)/// * `SIGSTOP`
[476](https://docs.rs#476)/// * `SIGILL`
[477](https://docs.rs#477)/// * `SIGFPE`
[478](https://docs.rs#478)/// * `SIGSEGV`
[479](https://docs.rs#479)///
[480](https://docs.rs#480)/// The first two are not possible to override (and the underlying C functions simply ignore all
[481](https://docs.rs#481)/// requests to do so, which smells of possible bugs, or return errors). The rest can be set, but
[482](https://docs.rs#482)/// generally needs very special handling to do so correctly (direct manipulation of the
[483](https://docs.rs#483)/// application's address space, `longjmp` and similar). Unless you know very well what you're
[484](https://docs.rs#484)/// doing, you'll shoot yourself into the foot and this library won't help you with that.
[485](https://docs.rs#485)///
[486](https://docs.rs#486)/// # Errors
[487](https://docs.rs#487)///
[488](https://docs.rs#488)/// Since the library manipulates signals using the low-level C functions, all these can return
[489](https://docs.rs#489)/// errors. Generally, the errors mean something like the specified signal does not exist on the
[490](https://docs.rs#490)/// given platform ‒ after a program is debugged and tested on a given OS, it should never return
[491](https://docs.rs#491)/// an error.
[492](https://docs.rs#492)///
[493](https://docs.rs#493)/// However, if an error *is* returned, there are no guarantees if the given action was registered
[494](https://docs.rs#494)/// or not.
[495](https://docs.rs#495)///
[496](https://docs.rs#496)/// # Safety
[497](https://docs.rs#497)///
[498](https://docs.rs#498)/// This function is unsafe, because the `action` is run inside a signal handler. While Rust is
[499](https://docs.rs#499)/// somewhat vague about the consequences of such, it is reasonably to assume that similar
[500](https://docs.rs#500)/// restrictions as specified in C or C++ apply.
[501](https://docs.rs#501)///
[502](https://docs.rs#502)/// In particular:
[503](https://docs.rs#503)///
[504](https://docs.rs#504)/// * Calling any OS functions that are not async-signal-safe as specified as POSIX is not allowed.
[505](https://docs.rs#505)/// * Accessing globals or thread-locals without synchronization is not allowed (however, mutexes
[506](https://docs.rs#506)///   are not within the async-signal-safe functions, therefore the synchronization is limited to
[507](https://docs.rs#507)///   using atomics).
[508](https://docs.rs#508)///
[509](https://docs.rs#509)/// The underlying reason is, signals are asynchronous (they can happen at arbitrary time) and are
[510](https://docs.rs#510)/// run in context of arbitrary thread (with some limited control of at which thread they can run).
[511](https://docs.rs#511)/// As a consequence, things like mutexes are prone to deadlocks, memory allocators can likely
[512](https://docs.rs#512)/// contain mutexes and the compiler doesn't expect the interruption during optimizations.
[513](https://docs.rs#513)///
[514](https://docs.rs#514)/// Things that generally are part of the async-signal-safe set (though check specifically) are
[515](https://docs.rs#515)/// routines to terminate the program, to further manipulate signals (by the low-level functions,
[516](https://docs.rs#516)/// not by this library) and to read and write file descriptors. The async-signal-safety is
[517](https://docs.rs#517)/// transitive - that is, a function composed only from computations (with local variables or with
[518](https://docs.rs#518)/// variables accessed with proper synchronizations) and other async-signal-safe functions is also
[519](https://docs.rs#519)/// safe.
[520](https://docs.rs#520)///
[521](https://docs.rs#521)/// As panicking from within a signal handler would be a panic across FFI boundary (which is
[522](https://docs.rs#522)/// undefined behavior), the passed handler must not panic.
[523](https://docs.rs#523)///
[524](https://docs.rs#524)/// Note that many innocently-looking functions do contain some of the forbidden routines (a lot of
[525](https://docs.rs#525)/// things lock or allocate).
[526](https://docs.rs#526)///
[527](https://docs.rs#527)/// If you find these limitations hard to satisfy, choose from the helper functions in the
[528](https://docs.rs#528)/// [signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) crate ‒ these provide safe interface to use some
[529](https://docs.rs#529)/// common signal handling patters.
[530](https://docs.rs#530)///
[531](https://docs.rs#531)/// # Race condition
[532](https://docs.rs#532)///
[533](https://docs.rs#533)/// Upon registering the first hook for a given signal into this library, there's a short race
[534](https://docs.rs#534)/// condition under the following circumstances:
[535](https://docs.rs#535)///
[536](https://docs.rs#536)/// * The program already has a signal handler installed for this particular signal (through some
[537](https://docs.rs#537)///   other library, possibly).
[538](https://docs.rs#538)/// * Concurrently, some other thread installs a different signal handler while it is being
[539](https://docs.rs#539)///   installed by this library.
[540](https://docs.rs#540)/// * At the same time, the signal is delivered.
[541](https://docs.rs#541)///
[542](https://docs.rs#542)/// Under such conditions signal-hook might wrongly "chain" to the older signal handler for a short
[543](https://docs.rs#543)/// while (until the registration is fully complete).
[544](https://docs.rs#544)///
[545](https://docs.rs#545)/// Note that the exact conditions of the race condition might change in future versions of the
[546](https://docs.rs#546)/// library. The recommended way to avoid it is to register signals before starting any additional
[547](https://docs.rs#547)/// threads, or at least not to register signals concurrently.
[548](https://docs.rs#548)///
[549](https://docs.rs#549)/// Alternatively, make sure all signals are handled through this library.
[550](https://docs.rs#550)///
[551](https://docs.rs#551)/// # Performance
[552](https://docs.rs#552)///
[553](https://docs.rs#553)/// Even when it is possible to repeatedly install and remove actions during the lifetime of a
[554](https://docs.rs#554)/// program, the installation and removal is considered a slow operation and should not be done
[555](https://docs.rs#555)/// very often. Also, there's limited (though huge) amount of distinct IDs (they are `u128`).
[556](https://docs.rs#556)///
[557](https://docs.rs#557)/// # Examples
[558](https://docs.rs#558)///
[559](https://docs.rs#559)/// ```rust
[560](https://docs.rs#560)/// extern crate signal_hook_registry;
[561](https://docs.rs#561)///
[562](https://docs.rs#562)/// use std::io::Error;
[563](https://docs.rs#563)/// use std::process;
[564](https://docs.rs#564)///
[565](https://docs.rs#565)/// fn main() -> Result<(), Error> {
[566](https://docs.rs#566)///     let signal = unsafe {
[567](https://docs.rs#567)///         signal_hook_registry::register(signal_hook::consts::SIGTERM, || process::abort())
[568](https://docs.rs#568)///     }?;
[569](https://docs.rs#569)///     // Stuff here...
[570](https://docs.rs#570)///     signal_hook_registry::unregister(signal); // Not really necessary.
[571](https://docs.rs#571)///     Ok(())
[572](https://docs.rs#572)/// }
[573](https://docs.rs#573)/// ```
[574](https://docs.rs#574)pub unsafe fn register<F>(signal: c_int, action: F) -> Result<SigId, Error>
[575](https://docs.rs#575)where
[576](https://docs.rs#576)    F: Fn() + Sync + Send + 'static,
[577](https://docs.rs#577){
[578](https://docs.rs#578)    register_sigaction_impl(signal, Arc::new(move |_: &_| action()))
[579](https://docs.rs#579)}
[580](https://docs.rs#580)
[581](https://docs.rs#581)/// Register a signal action.
[582](https://docs.rs#582)///
[583](https://docs.rs#583)/// This acts in the same way as [`register`], including the drawbacks, panics and performance
[584](https://docs.rs#584)/// characteristics. The only difference is the provided action accepts a [`siginfo_t`] argument,
[585](https://docs.rs#585)/// providing information about the received signal.
[586](https://docs.rs#586)///
[587](https://docs.rs#587)/// # Safety
[588](https://docs.rs#588)///
[589](https://docs.rs#589)/// See the details of [`register`].
[590](https://docs.rs#590)#[cfg(not(windows))]
[591](https://docs.rs#591)pub unsafe fn register_sigaction<F>(signal: c_int, action: F) -> Result<SigId, Error>
[592](https://docs.rs#592)where
[593](https://docs.rs#593)    F: Fn(&siginfo_t) + Sync + Send + 'static,
[594](https://docs.rs#594){
[595](https://docs.rs#595)    register_sigaction_impl(signal, Arc::new(action))

[623](https://docs.rs#623)/// Register a signal action without checking for forbidden signals.
[624](https://docs.rs#624)///
[625](https://docs.rs#625)/// This acts the same way as [`register_sigaction`], but without checking for the [`FORBIDDEN`]

[627](https://docs.rs#627)/// them.
[628](https://docs.rs#628)///
[629](https://docs.rs#629)/// Note that you really need to know what you're doing if you change eg. the `SIGSEGV` signal
[630](https://docs.rs#630)/// handler. Generally, you don't want to do that. But unlike the other functions here, this
[631](https://docs.rs#631)/// function still allows you to do it.

[636](https://docs.rs#636)#[cfg(not(windows))]
[637](https://docs.rs#637)pub unsafe fn register_unchecked<F>(signal: c_int, action: F) -> Result<SigId, Error>
[638](https://docs.rs#638)where
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    F: Fn(&siginfo_t) + Sync + Send + 'static,
[640](https://docs.rs#640){

[642](https://docs.rs#642)}
[643](https://docs.rs#643)
[644](https://docs.rs#644)unsafe fn register_unchecked_impl(signal: c_int, action: Arc<Action>) -> Result<SigId, Error> {
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    let globals = GlobalData::ensure();
[646](https://docs.rs#646)
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    let mut lock = globals.data.write();
[648](https://docs.rs#648)
[649](https://docs.rs#649)    let mut sigdata = SignalData::clone(&lock);
[650](https://docs.rs#650)    let id = ActionId(sigdata.next_id);
[651](https://docs.rs#651)    sigdata.next_id += 1;
[652](https://docs.rs#652)
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    if sigdata.signals.contains(&signal) {
[654](https://docs.rs#654)        let slot = sigdata.signals.get_mut(&signal).unwrap();
[655](https://docs.rs#655)        assert!(slot.actions.insert(id, action).is_none());
[656](https://docs.rs#656)    } else {
[657](https://docs.rs#657)        // While the sigaction/signal exchanges the old one atomically, we are not able to
[658](https://docs.rs#658)        // atomically store it somewhere a signal handler could read it. That poses a race
[659](https://docs.rs#659)        // condition where we could lose some signals delivered in between changing it and
[660](https://docs.rs#660)        // storing it.
[661](https://docs.rs#661)        //
[662](https://docs.rs#662)        // Therefore we first store the old one in the fallback storage. The fallback only
[663](https://docs.rs#663)        // covers the cases where the slot is not yet active and becomes "inert" after that,
[664](https://docs.rs#664)        // even if not removed (it may get overwritten by some other signal, but for that the
[665](https://docs.rs#665)        // mutex in globals.data must be unlocked here - and by that time we already stored the
[666](https://docs.rs#666)        // slot.
[667](https://docs.rs#667)        //
[668](https://docs.rs#668)        // And yes, this still leaves a short race condition when some other thread could
[669](https://docs.rs#669)        // replace the signal handler and we would be calling the outdated one for a short
[670](https://docs.rs#670)        // time, until we install the slot.
[671](https://docs.rs#671)        globals
[672](https://docs.rs#672)            .race_fallback
[673](https://docs.rs#673)            .write()
[674](https://docs.rs#674)            .store(Some(Prev::detect(signal)?));
[675](https://docs.rs#675)
[676](https://docs.rs#676)        let mut slot = Slot::new(signal)?;
[677](https://docs.rs#677)        slot.actions.insert(id, action);
[678](https://docs.rs#678)        sigdata.signals.insert(signal, slot);
[679](https://docs.rs#679)    }
[680](https://docs.rs#680)
[681](https://docs.rs#681)    lock.store(sigdata);
[682](https://docs.rs#682)
[683](https://docs.rs#683)    Ok(SigId { signal, action: id })
[684](https://docs.rs#684)}
[685](https://docs.rs#685)
[686](https://docs.rs#686)/// Removes a previously installed action.
[687](https://docs.rs#687)///
[688](https://docs.rs#688)/// This function does nothing if the action was already removed. It returns true if it was removed
[689](https://docs.rs#689)/// and false if the action wasn't found.
[690](https://docs.rs#690)///
[691](https://docs.rs#691)/// It can unregister all the actions installed by [`register`] as well as the ones from downstream
[692](https://docs.rs#692)/// crates (like [`signal-hook`](https://docs.rs/signal-hook)).
[693](https://docs.rs#693)///
[694](https://docs.rs#694)/// # Warning
[695](https://docs.rs#695)///
[696](https://docs.rs#696)/// This does *not* currently return the default/previous signal handler if the last action for a
[697](https://docs.rs#697)/// signal was just unregistered. That means that if you replaced for example `SIGTERM` and then
[698](https://docs.rs#698)/// removed the action, the program will effectively ignore `SIGTERM` signals from now on, not
[699](https://docs.rs#699)/// terminate on them as is the default action. This is OK if you remove it as part of a shutdown,
[700](https://docs.rs#700)/// but it is not recommended to remove termination actions during the normal runtime of
[701](https://docs.rs#701)/// application (unless the desired effect is to create something that can be terminated only by
[702](https://docs.rs#702)/// SIGKILL).
[703](https://docs.rs#703)pub fn unregister(id: SigId) -> bool {
[704](https://docs.rs#704)    let globals = GlobalData::ensure();
[705](https://docs.rs#705)    let mut replace = false;
[706](https://docs.rs#706)    let mut lock = globals.data.write();
[707](https://docs.rs#707)    let mut sigdata = SignalData::clone(&lock);
[708](https://docs.rs#708)    if let Some(slot) = sigdata.signals.get_mut(&id.signal) {
[709](https://docs.rs#709)        replace = slot.actions.remove(&id.action).is_some();
[710](https://docs.rs#710)    }
[711](https://docs.rs#711)    if replace {
[712](https://docs.rs#712)        lock.store(sigdata);
[713](https://docs.rs#713)    }
[714](https://docs.rs#714)    replace

# FORBIDDEN in signal_hook_registry - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/signal-hook-registry/1.4.8/signal_hook_registry/constant.FORBIDDEN.html

`pub const FORBIDDEN: &[`[c_int](https://docs.rs/libc/0.2.172/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/libc/primitives/type.c_int.html)];## Expand description

List of forbidden signals.

Some signals are impossible to replace according to POSIX and some are so special that this library refuses to handle them (eg. SIGSEGV). The routines panic in case registering one of these signals is attempted.

See [ register](https://docs.rs/fn.register.html).

# register in signal_hook_registry - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/signal-hook-registry/1.4.8/signal_hook_registry/fn.register.html

## Expand description

Registers an arbitrary action for the given signal.

This makes sure there’s a signal handler for the given signal. It then adds the action to the ones called each time the signal is delivered. If multiple actions are set for the same signal, all are called, in the order of registration.

If there was a previous signal handler for the given signal, it is chained ‒ it will be called as part of this library’s signal handler, before any actions set through this function.

On success, the function returns an ID that can be used to remove the action again with
[ unregister](https://docs.rs/fn.unregister.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If the signal is one of (see [ FORBIDDEN](https://docs.rs/constant.FORBIDDEN.html)):

- `SIGKILL`
- `SIGSTOP`
- `SIGILL`
- `SIGFPE`
- `SIGSEGV`

The first two are not possible to override (and the underlying C functions simply ignore all
requests to do so, which smells of possible bugs, or return errors). The rest can be set, but
generally needs very special handling to do so correctly (direct manipulation of the
application’s address space, `longjmp` and similar). Unless you know very well what you’re
doing, you’ll shoot yourself into the foot and this library won’t help you with that.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Since the library manipulates signals using the low-level C functions, all these can return errors. Generally, the errors mean something like the specified signal does not exist on the given platform ‒ after a program is debugged and tested on a given OS, it should never return an error.

However, if an error *is* returned, there are no guarantees if the given action was registered
or not.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

This function is unsafe, because the `action` is run inside a signal handler. While Rust is
somewhat vague about the consequences of such, it is reasonably to assume that similar
restrictions as specified in C or C++ apply.

In particular:

- Calling any OS functions that are not async-signal-safe as specified as POSIX is not allowed.
- Accessing globals or thread-locals without synchronization is not allowed (however, mutexes are not within the async-signal-safe functions, therefore the synchronization is limited to using atomics).

The underlying reason is, signals are asynchronous (they can happen at arbitrary time) and are run in context of arbitrary thread (with some limited control of at which thread they can run). As a consequence, things like mutexes are prone to deadlocks, memory allocators can likely contain mutexes and the compiler doesn’t expect the interruption during optimizations.

Things that generally are part of the async-signal-safe set (though check specifically) are routines to terminate the program, to further manipulate signals (by the low-level functions, not by this library) and to read and write file descriptors. The async-signal-safety is transitive - that is, a function composed only from computations (with local variables or with variables accessed with proper synchronizations) and other async-signal-safe functions is also safe.

As panicking from within a signal handler would be a panic across FFI boundary (which is undefined behavior), the passed handler must not panic.

Note that many innocently-looking functions do contain some of the forbidden routines (a lot of things lock or allocate).

If you find these limitations hard to satisfy, choose from the helper functions in the
[signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) crate ‒ these provide safe interface to use some
common signal handling patters.

[§](https://docs.rs#race-condition)Race condition

Upon registering the first hook for a given signal into this library, there’s a short race condition under the following circumstances:

- The program already has a signal handler installed for this particular signal (through some other library, possibly).
- Concurrently, some other thread installs a different signal handler while it is being installed by this library.
- At the same time, the signal is delivered.

Under such conditions signal-hook might wrongly “chain” to the older signal handler for a short while (until the registration is fully complete).

Note that the exact conditions of the race condition might change in future versions of the library. The recommended way to avoid it is to register signals before starting any additional threads, or at least not to register signals concurrently.

Alternatively, make sure all signals are handled through this library.

[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

Even when it is possible to repeatedly install and remove actions during the lifetime of a
program, the installation and removal is considered a slow operation and should not be done
very often. Also, there’s limited (though huge) amount of distinct IDs (they are `u128`).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
extern crate signal_hook_registry;
use std::io::Error;
use std::process;
fn main() -> Result<(), Error> {
    let signal = unsafe {
        signal_hook_registry::register(signal_hook::consts::SIGTERM, || process::abort())
    }?;
    // Stuff here...
    signal_hook_registry::unregister(signal); // Not really necessary.
    Ok(())
}
```

# register_unchecked in signal_hook_registry - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/signal-hook-registry/1.4.8/signal_hook_registry/fn.register_unchecked.html

## Expand description

Register a signal action without checking for forbidden signals.

This acts the same way as [ register_sigaction](https://docs.rs/fn.register_sigaction.html), but without checking for the

[signals. All the signals passed are registered and it is up to the caller to make some sense of them.](https://docs.rs/constant.FORBIDDEN.html)

`FORBIDDEN`Note that you really need to know what you’re doing if you change eg. the `SIGSEGV` signal
handler. Generally, you don’t want to do that. But unlike the other functions here, this
function still allows you to do it.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

See the details of [ register](https://docs.rs/fn.register.html).

# unregister in signal_hook_registry - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/signal-hook-registry/1.4.8/signal_hook_registry/fn.unregister.html

## Expand description

Removes a previously installed action.

This function does nothing if the action was already removed. It returns true if it was removed and false if the action wasn’t found.

It can unregister all the actions installed by [ register](https://docs.rs/fn.register.html) as well as the ones from downstream
crates (like

[).](https://docs.rs/signal-hook)

`signal-hook`[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

This does *not* currently return the default/previous signal handler if the last action for a
signal was just unregistered. That means that if you replaced for example `SIGTERM` and then
removed the action, the program will effectively ignore `SIGTERM` signals from now on, not
terminate on them as is the default action. This is OK if you remove it as part of a shutdown,
but it is not recommended to remove termination actions during the normal runtime of
application (unless the desired effect is to create something that can be terminated only by
SIGKILL).

# signal_hook_registry - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/signal-hook-registry/latest/signal_hook_registry/

## Expand description

Backend of the [signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) crate.

The [signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) crate tries to provide an API to the unix signals, which are a global
resource. Therefore, it is desirable an application contains just one version of the crate
which manages this global resource. But that makes it impossible to make breaking changes in
the API.

Therefore, this crate provides very minimal and low level API to the signals that is unlikely
to have to change, while there may be multiple versions of the [signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) that all use this
low-level API to provide different versions of the high level APIs.

It is also possible some other crates might want to build a completely different API. This split allows these crates to still reuse the same low-level routines in this crate instead of going to the (much more dangerous) unix calls.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-this-crate-provides)What this crate provides

The only thing this crate does is multiplexing the signals. An application or library can add or remove callbacks and have multiple callbacks for the same signal.

It handles dispatching the callbacks and managing them in a way that uses only the
[async-signal-safe](http://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal-safety.7.html) functions inside the signal handler. Note that the callbacks are still run
inside the signal handler, so it is up to the caller to ensure they are also
[async-signal-safe](http://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal-safety.7.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#what-this-is-for)What this is for

This is a building block for other libraries creating reasonable abstractions on top of
signals. The [signal-hook](https://docs.rs/signal-hook) is the generally preferred way if you need to handle signals in your
application and provides several safe patterns of doing so.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version-compatibility)Rust version compatibility

Currently builds on 1.26.0 an newer and this is very unlikely to change. However, tests require dependencies that don’t build there, so tests need newer Rust version (they are run on stable).

Note that this ancient version of rustc no longer compiles current versions of `libc`. If you
want to use rustc this old, you need to force your dependency resolution to pick old enough
version of `libc` (`0.2.156` was found to work, but newer ones may too).

[§](https://docs.rs#portability)Portability

This crate includes a limited support for Windows, based on `signal`/`raise` in the CRT.
There are differences in both API and behavior:

- Due to lack of `siginfo_t`, we don’t provide`register_sigaction`or`register_unchecked`.
- Due to lack of signal blocking, there’s a race condition.
After the call to `signal`, there’s a moment where we miss a signal. That means when you register a handler, there may be a signal which invokes neither the default handler or the handler you register.
- Handlers registered by `signal`in Windows are cleared on first signal. To match behavior in other platforms, we re-register the handler each time the handler is called, but there’s a moment where we miss a handler. That means when you receive two signals in a row, there may be a signal which invokes the default handler, nevertheless you certainly have registered the handler.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [SigId](https://docs.rs/struct.SigId.html)
- An ID of registered action.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [FORBIDDEN](https://docs.rs/constant.FORBIDDEN.html)
- List of forbidden signals.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [register](https://docs.rs/fn.register.html)- ⚠
- Registers an arbitrary action for the given signal.
- [register_](https://docs.rs/fn.register_sigaction.html)- sigaction - ⚠
- Register a signal action.
- [register_](https://docs.rs/fn.register_signal_unchecked.html)- signal_ - unchecked - ⚠
- Register a signal action without checking for forbidden signals.
- [register_](https://docs.rs/fn.register_unchecked.html)- unchecked - ⚠
- Register a signal action without checking for forbidden signals.
- [unregister](https://docs.rs/fn.unregister.html)
- Removes a previously installed action.

# libc 0.2.186 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/libc/^0.2

# libc - Raw FFI bindings to platforms' system libraries

`libc` provides all of the definitions necessary to easily interoperate with C
code (or "C-like" code) on each of the platforms that Rust supports. This
includes type definitions (e.g. `c_int`), constants (e.g. `EINVAL`) as well as
function headers (e.g. `malloc`).

This crate exports all underlying platform types, functions, and constants under
the crate root, so all items are accessible as `libc::foo`. The types and values
of all the exported APIs match the platform that libc is compiled for.

Windows API bindings are not included in this crate. If you are looking for
WinAPI bindings, consider using crates like [windows-sys](https://docs.rs/windows-sys).

More detailed information about the design of this library can be found in its
[associated RFC](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/HEAD/text/1291-promote-libc.md).

## v1.0 Roadmap

Currently, `libc` has two active branches: `main` for the upcoming v1.0 release,
and `libc-0.2` for the currently published version. By default all pull requests
should target `main`; once reviewed, they can be cherry picked to the `libc-0.2`
branch if needed.

We will stop making new v0.2 releases once v1.0 is released.

See the section in [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://docs.rs/CONTRIBUTING.md#v10-roadmap) for more
details.

## Usage

Add the following to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
## Features

-
`std`: by default`libc`links to the standard library. Disable this feature to remove this dependency and be able to use`libc`in`#![no_std]`crates.
-
`extra_traits`: all`struct`s implemented in`libc`are`Copy`and`Clone`. This feature derives`Debug`,`Eq`,`Hash`, and`PartialEq`.

The following features are deprecated:

- `use_std`: this is equivalent to- `std`
- `const-extern-fn`: this is now enabled by default
- `align`: this is now enabled by default

## Rust version support

The minimum supported Rust toolchain version is currently **Rust 1.65**.

Increases to the MSRV are allowed to change without a major (i.e. semver- breaking) release in order to avoid a ripple effect in the ecosystem. A policy for when this may change is a work in progress.

`libc` may continue to compile with Rust versions older than the current MSRV
but this is not guaranteed.

the platforms on which
